doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

title: Riffing fading, and new players in a head band
summary: Younger players don't riff; Foster plans to restore head sections; schooled players struggle without ears.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It’s not, like you said, it’s not as prevalent now because the younger guys are not that acquainted with that kind of thing. You know they’ve come through schools and outfits where they don’t do that much “riffing” we call it. But back during the 50’s when I joined this band, and even before I joined this band, you know like you had to be able to vest up some kind of riffs in order to make the gig.

Exactly. At some point or another, every now and then one would write out an arrangement. A written arrangement. And then leave space open during solo sections for riffs to be done behind solos. That’s hardly done any more either. It slips my mind to do it. I’m so taken with orchestrations and textures and colors that I want to fill it up with everything that comes out of my head. But I’m going to get back to that — letting the fellas help with these head sections of written arrangements.
You’ve kind of got to let go a little bit and let them do some of it.
Yeah. Cause that’s what this band did in the early days.
Yeah, there were a lot of head arrangements when I first came in this band.
Was it, when you, like if a band that does head arrangements like that, is it a lot harder for a new guy to come into the band and find his place?
It depends on the new guy himself.

Yeah. It depends on where he’s playing from, you know? If he’s sprung from Berklee College or something like that, it’s going to be difficult for him, you know because he’s been well versed in written music, you know? And the minute you take him away from that, you’re saying what the hell is going on?
There’s a lot to be said for the ears, right?

Definitely. You have to have an ear so that you can catch up on a riff or a lick after the first time it’s played. The guy that sets the riff plays it the first time, the second time the whole section plays it. Verbatim.
